introduction.en: The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is a mandatory percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that banks must maintain as cash with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). It is a key quantitative tool under the RBI Act, 1934.
introduction.hi: The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is a mandatory percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that banks must maintain as cash with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). It is a key quantitative tool under the RBI Act, 1934.

body.en: CRR acts as a primary instrument to regulate liquidity in the banking system. By increasing the CRR, the RBI reduces the lendable resources of banks, thereby curbing credit growth and controlling inflation. Conversely, a reduction in CRR injects liquidity, encouraging investment and economic growth. It directly influences the money multiplier effect, as higher reserves limit the capacity of banks to create credit.
body.hi: CRR acts as a primary instrument to regulate liquidity in the banking system. By increasing the CRR, the RBI reduces the lendable resources of banks, thereby curbing credit growth and controlling inflation. Conversely, a reduction in CRR injects liquidity, encouraging investment and economic growth. It directly influences the money multiplier effect, as higher reserves limit the capacity of banks to create credit.

conclusion.en: Thus, CRR serves as a vital instrument for the RBI to maintain price stability and ensure the health of the financial system.
conclusion.hi: Thus, CRR serves as a vital instrument for the RBI to maintain price stability and ensure the health of the financial system.

valueAddition.en: CRR is currently maintained on a fortnightly average basis to provide operational flexibility to banks.
